questions.q: Why does NVLink exist as a separate interconnect from the standard PCIe bus inside a GPU server?
options: PCIe's roughly 64GB/s bandwidth is nowhere near enough for distributed training's gradient and activation traffic, so NVLink provides a direct, much higher-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU path that bypasses PCIe and the CPU
NVLink is only a marketing term for PCIe running at a higher clock speed
PCIe is actually faster than NVLink, but NVLink uses less power
NVLink exists solely to connect GPUs to storage devices, not to other GPUs
questions.explain: Standard PCIe tops out around 64GB/s, far too little for the volume of GPU-to-GPU traffic distributed training generates. NVLink, often combined with NVSwitch, delivers hundreds of GB/s to nearly 1TB/s per GPU instead.

questions.q: What does GPUDirect RDMA specifically enable in a multi-machine training cluster?
options: It compresses gradients before sending them over Ethernet
It lets one machine's GPU write data directly into another machine's GPU memory, without routing through either machine's CPU or main system memory
It replaces InfiniBand entirely with a CPU-based networking stack
It only works for storing checkpoints, not for gradient synchronization
questions.explain: GPUDirect RDMA removes the CPU and main memory from the path entirely, cutting latency and CPU overhead for cross-machine gradient exchange — a major reason InfiniBand plus RDMA is standard for between-machine training traffic.

questions.q: What does "bisection bandwidth" measure in a training cluster's network topology, and why does it matter?
options: The total storage capacity of the cluster's parallel filesystem
The number of GPUs a single server chassis can physically hold

The bandwidth available between the two halves of a cluster if it were split in two; low bisection bandwidth creates a bottleneck exactly where large collective operations like AllReduce need to move the most data
The clock speed of the switches used in the network fabric
questions.explain: Bisection bandwidth reveals whether a topology can actually sustain large collective communication patterns at scale. Fat-tree and rail-optimized designs exist specifically to keep this bandwidth high as clusters grow.

questions.q: Why can adding more GPUs to a training job stop improving training speed, even when every GPU is individually fast?
options: GPUs have a hard-coded limit of 8 units per training job regardless of network design
More GPUs causes the optimizer to recompute the entire model from scratch each step
Adding more GPUs always increases speed with no exceptions; this scenario cannot occur in practice

As GPU count grows, each GPU's share of per-step compute shrinks, but AllReduce still has to move every gradient across the network every step — past a certain scale, communication time can exceed compute time
questions.explain: Communication scales differently than compute as GPU count grows. Once gradient-synchronization time exceeds per-step compute time, the network — not the GPUs — becomes the limiting factor on training throughput.

questions.q: Why does NCCL implement AllReduce using ring or tree-structured communication patterns instead of a naive "everyone send to everyone" approach?
options: Ring and tree algorithms are specifically designed to use the available network topology efficiently, keeping gradient synchronization from dominating total training time as cluster size grows
Ring and tree patterns were chosen arbitrarily and offer no measurable advantage over naive broadcasting
NCCL only supports ring and tree patterns because InfiniBand hardware cannot route any other pattern
A naive all-to-all pattern is actually faster, but NCCL avoids it for licensing reasons
questions.explain: Naive all-to-all communication doesn't scale efficiently with cluster size. Ring and tree-structured AllReduce algorithms are engineered to match the physical topology and minimize the communication overhead that would otherwise bottleneck training.
